passage: At the tube-well after school, Vishal was still buzzing about the block-level maths quiz. "Rajni, you were amazing! Honestly, you think like a boy," he said, grinning, and held up his hand for a high five. Rajni didn't lift hers. "What does that mean?" "It's a compliment! Girls usually..." He stopped. Her face had gone very still. "Usually what?" she asked quietly, and picked up her bucket. Vishal walked home with his cheeks burning. He had meant it as the best praise he knew. At dinner he told his mother, who put down her ladle. "Would you like it if someone said you were clever for a boy?" Vishal stared at his roti. He hadn't thought of it like that at all.

qa.q: Which quiz was Vishal still excited about?
qa.a: The block-level maths quiz.

qa.q: Why were Vishal's cheeks burning on the walk home?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and confused; he had meant it as the best praise he knew and was shocked that it hurt Rajni.

qa.q: What could Vishal do the next day at the tube-well?
qa.a: He could tell Rajni she was amazing, full stop, and say sorry that "like a boy" made it sound as if girls usually aren't.

qa.q: How might Rajni have heard "you think like a boy"?
qa.a: Rajni likely heard that her win was an exception for a girl, which takes the credit away from her own mind.

grounding: A teenager compliments a girl by saying she thinks like a boy, sincerely meaning it kindly, and is shocked to learn it hurt.

passage: In the school library in Edinburgh, Freya leaned over to Alejandro's table with a warm smile. "I just wanted to say, you're honestly so inspiring. Like, just coming to school every day in your wheelchair." Alejandro looked up from his chemistry. "I come to school to do chemistry. Same as you." "No, I mean, it's brave." "It's a ramp and a lift," he said, not unkindly, and went back to his book. Freya's face went hot. She had rehearsed it on the bus, sure it would make his day. On the walk home she replayed it: she'd praised him for existing, not for anything he'd done. That evening she messaged him: "Sorry about earlier. I meant it kindly, but I get why it landed wrong." He replied: "Thanks. You can say my titration was inspiring though."

qa.q: What was Alejandro studying in the library?
qa.a: He was studying chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Freya's face go hot?
qa.a: She was shocked and embarrassed; she had rehearsed the compliment, sure it would make his day, and it landed wrong.

qa.q: Which part of Freya's apology made it work?
qa.a: She didn't defend her intent or ask for comfort; she named that it landed wrong and said sorry.

qa.q: What might Alejandro's joke about his titration tell Freya?
qa.a: It suggests he's happy to be praised for what he actually does, and that things are still friendly between them.

grounding: A teenager praises a classmate in a wheelchair as inspiring for simply attending school, meaning it kindly, and learns the effect was not kind.

passage: In the study hall of the residential school, Damini leaned across the desk to read Lalremsiami's essay and gasped. "This is so good! Honestly, I thought sports-quota kids only cared about training." She laughed, meaning it as a compliment. Lalremsiami closed the notebook. "I'm in the reading club too. Since Class 6." "I know, I just meant..." "You meant you were surprised." The warden's bell rang for lights out. Damini lay awake on her bunk, stunned. She had been trying to be nice. She replayed the words and heard, for the first time, the "only" in them. In the morning she found Lalremsiami at the water cooler. "I'm sorry. I put you in a box. The essay's just good." Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "Okay. Thanks for coming back."

qa.q: Since when has Lalremsiami been in the reading club?
qa.a: Since Class 6.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she lay awake on her bunk?
qa.a: She was stunned and uneasy; she had meant to be nice and only now heard the "only" in her own words.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Damini, and what made her morning apology work?
qa.a: Hearing the "only" was the turning point; the apology worked because it named what she did, putting Lalremsiami in a box, without asking for reassurance.

qa.q: What might "Thanks for coming back" show about how Lalremsiami felt?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was hurt, but valued that Damini came back to own it instead of letting it slide.

grounding: A student compliments a classmate's essay through a stereotype about sports-quota students, meaning well, and is shocked to realise it hurt.

passage:
Sahil,
I tried to say this at the bus stop and it came out wrong, so I'm writing it.
At the science fair, when the judges praised your bridge, I said really loudly, "Obviously! It's in his blood. His family runs the cycle shop, he was born to fix things." I meant it as the biggest compliment. I was proud of you.
Then you didn't talk the whole ride home, and Tanya told me later what you'd said to her: that you spent three weeks on the load calculations, and I made it sound like your hands did it and your head didn't.
Honestly, I didn't see it. I was shocked. I kept thinking, but I was being nice!
Being nice and landing nice aren't the same thing, I get that now. The calculations were yours. I'm sorry I made it about the shop.
Hemant

qa.q: How long did Sahil spend on the load calculations?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why was Hemant so shocked to learn the comment had hurt?
qa.a: Hemant sincerely meant "it's in his blood" as the biggest compliment and felt proud, so it came as a real surprise that it had erased Sahil's hard thinking.

qa.q: At the fair, what could Hemant have chosen to say instead?
qa.a: Hemant could have praised the actual work, something like "Sahil did all the load calculations", instead of tying the bridge to the family's cycle shop.

qa.q: How did the comment look from Sahil's side?
qa.a: To Sahil, three weeks of careful maths was turned into an inherited knack, as if the family shop mattered more than Sahil's own mind.

grounding: A student praises Sahil with a stereotype about the family trade, sincerely meaning it kindly, and is shocked to learn the effect hurt.

passage: Okay, Rukmini, you asked what I learnt this term, so here's the embarrassing one. I'm Gargi, and I'm the joker in our group, right? Everyone knows me for it. During the group project, Francis kept the only calculator on his desk, and I said, "Classic only child, never learnt to share," and did a little spoilt-baby voice. Everybody laughed. Francis laughed too, sort of. I thought that was the end of it. Two days later his friend told me Francis went home upset. Apparently he's heard that line since forever, and he's the one who photocopies his notes for half the class. I was honestly shocked. I kept saying, "But it was a joke! I like him!" And I do. That's the weird part. I meant it as teasing between friends, and it still landed as one more person calling him selfish. I said sorry the next morning, with no jokes attached.

qa.q: What did Gargi say when Francis kept the calculator?
qa.a: "Classic only child, never learnt to share," in a little spoilt-baby voice.

qa.q: What does Gargi's "But it was a joke! I like him!" show about how Gargi felt?
qa.a: Gargi was genuinely shocked and a bit defensive, because the joke came from affection and Gargi never imagined it could feel like an insult.

qa.q: What turning point shows Gargi learning, and what made the apology work?
qa.a: Gargi apologised the next morning with no jokes attached, which took the hurt seriously instead of explaining the good intent again.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis to hear the only-child line once more?
qa.a: Francis has heard it forever, so even from a friend it feels like one more person calling him selfish, despite sharing notes with half the class.

grounding: A teenager teases a friend with an only-child stereotype, sure it is friendly, and is shocked to discover the joke hurt.

passage: In the Madrid school canteen, Pablo, fifteen, sat across from Elif, who'd moved from Istanbul last year. She'd just aced the history test. "You're so clever," he said, grinning. "Honestly, you don't seem Turkish at all. You're really modern." He meant it kindly. He'd heard his uncle say similar things about his Turkish colleagues. Elif's smile froze. She put down her fork. "What does that mean? Turkish people aren't modern?" Pablo blinked. "No, I just meant... it was a compliment." "It didn't feel like one," she said quietly and went to sit with her friends. Pablo sat there, stunned. He'd only wanted to be nice. That night he replayed the words and heard them the way Elif had. His face burned. The compliment had carried an insult inside it.

qa.q: What had Elif just aced?
qa.a: She'd just aced the history test.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel when Elif walked away?
qa.a: Pablo felt stunned and confused, sure he'd only meant to be nice, and later embarrassed as he understood.

qa.q: What could Pablo do the next day?
qa.a: Pablo could apologise to Elif for how it came across, without insisting he meant well, and simply praise her work next time.

qa.q: How did Elif experience Pablo's "compliment"?
qa.a: Elif felt hurt and insulted, since it implied Turkish people aren't normally modern.

grounding: A student gives a compliment based on a stereotype, sincerely thinking it friendly, and is shocked to learn it hurt.

passage: In the school library, Saurabh, sixteen, leaned over to Swati, who'd just topped the chemistry test. "Bihari brain!" he said, laughing. "You guys always top the exams." He meant it as praise; his cousin said the same about Bihari toppers in Kota. Swati didn't laugh. "So I topped because I'm Bihari? Not because I studied every night?" Saurabh's grin faded. "No, I didn't mean it like that." "It's what everyone says," Swati said. "Like it's in my blood and not my work." The librarian looked up. Saurabh felt his cheeks heat. He'd honestly thought he was being nice. "Sorry," he mumbled. Swati nodded stiffly and turned back to her book. Saurabh sat down, confused and embarrassed, trying to understand how a compliment had landed so badly.

qa.q: What did Saurabh say when Swati topped the test?
qa.a: He said, "Bihari brain!"

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when his grin faded?
qa.a: Saurabh felt confused and embarrassed, shocked that what he meant as praise had hurt.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do to repair this?
qa.a: He could listen to Swati's point, apologise for the effect, and in future praise her for her hard work rather than her background.

qa.q: How did Swati experience Saurabh's comment?
qa.a: Swati felt her hard work was dismissed, as if her success came from being Bihari rather than from studying every night.

grounding: A student makes a stereotype-based compliment thinking it friendly, and is shocked to learn it hurt because it dismissed his classmate's effort.

passage:
Deepak,
I've been thinking about Friday. When you solved that maths problem on the board, I said, "Of course, South Indians are always good at maths." Everyone laughed, and I thought I was complimenting you. Then I saw your face.
Later Tina told me you'd been up till two every night practising. And that people say that to you all the time, like your work doesn't count.
I honestly didn't mean it badly. But I get now that it doesn't matter what I meant. It still took something away from you.
I'm sorry. You're good at maths because you work hard, not because of where you're from. I won't say that kind of thing again.
Mridul

qa.q: Until what time had Deepak been practising?
qa.a: Deepak had been up till two every night practising.

qa.q: How does Mridul feel after hearing from Tina?
qa.a: Mridul feels shocked and sorry, realising a well-meant comment still hurt Deepak.

qa.q: What does Mridul's letter do to repair the hurt?
qa.a: It names exactly what was said, accepts the effect regardless of intent, credits Deepak's hard work, and promises to change.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Deepak might feel relieved and respected that Mridul understood and acknowledged Deepak's effort.

grounding: A student realises a well-meant stereotype-based compliment hurt a classmate by erasing the classmate's effort, and apologises.

passage:
You want to know the worst compliment I ever gave? I'm Arohi, and this was last month.
Aadhya came to the class party in a yellow lehenga, and she looked lovely. I said, loudly, "You look so pretty even though you're dark!" I really meant it as praise. I even thought I was being nice.
Her face went still. She said "thanks" and moved to the other corner.
Later her best friend told me Aadhya had cried in the washroom. I was shocked. I kept saying, "But I was being nice!"
Then her friend asked me, "Why 'even though'?" And I had no answer.
I apologised the next day. Just sorry, no excuses.

qa.q: What did Aadhya wear to the class party?
qa.a: She wore a yellow lehenga.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel on hearing that Aadhya had cried?
qa.a: Arohi felt shocked and confused, since the compliment was meant kindly, and then ashamed.

qa.q: What did Arohi do right afterwards?
qa.a: Arohi apologised the next day without excuses, taking responsibility for the effect instead of defending the intent.

qa.q: What was it like for Aadhya to hear that compliment in front of the class?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and singled out, since the words suggested her skin colour was something to overcome.

grounding: Shows a student giving a compliment built on a stereotype, sincerely meaning it kindly, and being shocked to learn it hurt.

passage:
Monday: In the canteen, Minakshi grinned at Harish, who had moved from Kerala. "Our coconut boy! You must put coconut in everything, na?" The table laughed. Harish laughed too.
Wednesday: Minakshi said it again in class when Harish got a question right. "Coconut power!" Harish smiled, but he didn't look up.
The next Monday: Harish stopped her at the gate. "Minakshi, can I tell you something? I know you mean it nicely. But I'm just Harish. Every time you say 'coconut boy', everyone looks at me like I'm a joke about Kerala."
Minakshi went red. "I thought it was friendly."
"I know. That's why I'm telling you."

qa.q: Where had Harish moved from?
qa.a: He had moved from Kerala.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel when Harish stopped her at the gate?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and surprised, because she had thought the nickname was friendly.

qa.q: What would you advise Minakshi to do now?
qa.a: Say sorry, drop the nickname, and call Harish by his name, without explaining how she meant well.

qa.q: What was it like for Harish when the table laughed?
qa.a: Harish laughed along but felt uncomfortable and reduced to a joke about where he comes from.

grounding: Shows a student making a friendly-seeming joke based on a regional stereotype, and being shocked to learn it hurt, over several days.

passage:
Sunaina, you worry you said something wrong to your friend? Let your Mama tell you a story. I'm Harish. At fifteen, a new boy joined our Nagpur school from a village near Wardha. He was quick in class, quicker than me.
One day I clapped him on the back and said, "You don't seem like a village boy at all!" I meant it as the biggest praise I had.
He stopped smiling. "What does a village boy seem like?" he asked.
I didn't know what to say. I had meant it kindly. He had heard that his village was something to escape.
I said sorry the next day. We became friends after that. But I've never said "you don't seem like" again.

qa.q: Where did the new boy come from?
qa.a: He came from a village near Wardha.

qa.q: What did young Harish feel when the boy asked, "What does a village boy seem like?"
qa.a: He felt shocked and unsure, realising his kind words had hurt.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Harish's story?
qa.a: Saying sorry the next day; it showed he took the hurt seriously, and they became friends.

qa.q: How might the new boy have heard Harish's praise?
qa.a: He probably heard it as saying his village was something to hide or escape, which stung.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a teenager giving praise based on a stereotype about village people and being surprised to learn it hurt.

passage: The fest was in two hours and the science stall still had no labels. Noor was cutting, Naveen was writing, and the hall was so loud they had to shout. "Naveen, you do the formula chart," Noor called. "You're Tamil, you guys are all maths geniuses!" She meant it warmly; she'd heard it all her life as a compliment. Naveen's marker stopped. "I'm actually bad at maths," he said flatly, and walked off to find tape. Noor blinked. Later, as they packed up, he said, "People say that to me every week. When I get a low mark, it feels like I've failed my whole family's state." Noor's face went hot. "I thought it was a nice thing to say." "I know," he said. "That's why I'm telling you."

qa.q: How long was it until the fest when the stall had no labels?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when Naveen explained?
qa.a: Noor was shocked and embarrassed; she had meant the remark kindly and never imagined it hurt.

qa.q: What would you advise Noor to say next?

qa.q: What is it like for Naveen to hear the same compliment every week?

passage: At the colony's inter-school debate practice, Parveen couldn't stop smiling at Nitin's speech. He had argued so clearly that even the coach clapped. Afterwards, she caught him at the gate. "You were amazing! Honestly, I'd never have guessed your father drives an auto, you speak so well." She meant it as the highest praise. Nitin's smile slipped. "Why wouldn't I speak well?" "No, I just meant..." She stopped. What had she meant? "You meant people like me usually don't," he said quietly, and got on his cycle. Parveen stood at the gate, stunned. She replayed her own words and heard them the way he had. That night she typed a message three times before sending: "I'm sorry. You're a great speaker. Full stop."

qa.q: Where did Parveen catch Nitin after the speech?
qa.a: At the gate.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling as she stood at the gate?
qa.a: She felt stunned and ashamed, realising her compliment carried an assumption that hurt Nitin even though she meant it kindly.

qa.q: Why is Parveen's final message a good repair?

qa.q: How does Nitin see the compliment?
qa.a: He hears it as saying that people from his background usually can't speak well, so the praise feels like a put-down.

grounding: Illustrates a student whose well-meant compliment rests on a stereotype and who is shocked to learn it hurt.

passage: "Dolma! Momo queen!" Vijay called across the art room. A few kids laughed. "Hi," Dolma said, not looking up from her painting. "What, you don't like momos?" "I like them fine." "So why the face?" Dolma put her brush down. "Vijay, you call me that every day. My family's from Dharamshala, and people have called me momo, chinki, Nepali, all my life. I know you mean it as a friendly nickname." Vijay's grin vanished. "I... it's a food. I thought it was cute." "It's cute once. Every day, it's like I'm just a food to people." "I honestly didn't know." "I know. That's why I'm saying it to you and not to them." Vijay nodded slowly. "Dolma, then. Just Dolma."

qa.q: Where is Dolma's family from?
qa.a: Dharamshala.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Dolma explained the nickname?
qa.a: He was shocked and embarrassed; he sincerely thought the nickname was cute and friendly, not hurtful.

qa.q: What did Vijay do right at the end?
qa.a: He listened without arguing and agreed to call her just Dolma, adjusting instead of defending himself.

qa.q: Why might Dolma choose to tell Vijay rather than the others?
qa.a: She seems to see Vijay as someone who means well and might actually change, so telling him feels worth the effort.

grounding: Shows a student using a stereotype-based nickname as friendly teasing and being surprised to learn the effect.

passage: Last Holi our whole building played in the parking lot, and I thought I was being funny. Kunal from the fourth floor came out grinning, and I shouted, "Lucky you! With your dark skin the colour won't even show!" A few people laughed. I laughed too; I honestly thought it was a friendly joke, like teasing someone for being tall. Kunal's grin stayed, but he went home early. Two days later his sister stopped me by the lift. "Simran," she said, very calmly, "Kunal has heard jokes about his skin his whole life, from relatives, strangers, school. Yours was just the newest." My face burned. I kept saying, "But I didn't mean it like that." She said, "I know. It still landed like that." That evening I knocked on their door and said sorry to Kunal properly, without explaining myself.

qa.q: When did Kunal's sister stop Simran by the lift?
qa.a: Two days later.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Kunal's sister explained?
qa.a: Simran felt shocked and ashamed, face burning, because a joke meant kindly had actually hurt.

qa.q: What did Simran get right in the end?
qa.a: Simran apologised to Kunal properly the same evening, without explaining or defending the intention.

qa.q: What might the joke have felt like for Kunal?
qa.a: It probably stung as one more in a lifetime of remarks about his skin, even though he kept grinning and just went home early.

grounding: A teenager makes a Holi joke about a neighbour's skin, sincerely thinking it friendly, and is shocked to learn it hurt.
